utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours; good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I would first remind you, you are still under your oath. Is counsel ready to continue his cross-examination of Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. May I begin, Your Honour? May I begin, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, yesterday we broke off as we were discussing the relevance of a piece of information that evolved during the course of the work of the Tribunal and that is the number of the casualties in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you recall that we talked about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I am not going to discuss the numbers back and forth with you. Nobody would like to do that. However, I with like to point to the importance of such a piece of information and how important it is for the Tribunal, at the beginning of its work, to have such a fact and that all historical facts are important, including this one, so that the Chamber could reach adequate and proper decisions, and this is the reason why I was dealing with the number of casualties. For example, the first piece of information that was taken as some sort of basis, and you agreed that you had heard about that, the figure of 20.000 Muslims killed and 40.000 Muslim women raped, points to the kind of war that was waged in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the second piece of information towards the end of the work of the Tribunal on which the demographers agree, and I have received the exact figures, you know the approximate ones just as I do but now we have the exact figures, 63.000 Bosniaks -- 63.000 Bosniaks, 24.000 Serbs, and 7.700 Croats, giving a total figure of 97.207 victims, when we break it down to the ethnic structure, they are arranged in order according to the ethnic structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina's population, perhaps not quite exactly but more or less in that order. All three peoples had civilian casualties of the war. The Tribunal tried civilian Bosniaks, Croats, and Muslims, and in all indictments and in all judgements all the accused were charged with committing criminal acts against civilians. So this particular piece of information changes the character and the nature of the war. This piece of information, among other data, indicates that there was an ethnic civil conflict in this area in which all three peoples suffered losses. My question to you, Mr. Donia, can you confirm one fact for me? In this I'm going to call this Bermuda triangle of three peoples, Serbs, Croats and Muslims, when I say the black Bermuda triangle, I mean the participation in the war. In that triangle all possible combinations of mutual conflicts occurred. If you permit. Serbs waged war against Muslims -- or, rather, Muslims and Serbs against each other, Muslims and Croats waged war against each other. You know about that part of the war. Croats and Serbs waged war against one another. Muslims, supporters of Alija Izetbegovic waged war with the followers of Fikret Abdic. Also, Muslims waged war together against the Serbs. I tried to find some more combinations, and I established that the only option is that the Serbs and Muslims did not wage war against Croats and Serbs against Serbs. They did -- that did not happen. So are you aware of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Your Honour, I'm really am sorry but I think I'd better say it now, once and once only. It's not a question, it's long speech giving evidence. One of your guidelines, I've just been reminded, was the parties are to avoid lengthy, complicated or combined questions. Please so that I don't have to interrupt again, can I ask Mr. Cvijetic to ask simple, one-fact questions, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We would agree, Mr. Cvijetic, and certainly it's normally for the witnesses to bring evidence and not the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you agree with this combination of conflicts between the parties, that question -- that part of the question at least was short and clear.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not to me. I would have to go back piece and piece and see which of that was -- I would agree with and which I would not. I'm afraid I don't understand it as a direct question and can't really -- can't really answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to divide the question. Did Serbs and Muslims wage war against one another?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Muslims and Croats wage war against one another at a certain point during the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Croats and Serbs wage war against one another?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Muslims and Croats wage war together against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Muslims and Muslims wage war against one another, the followers of Alija Izetbegovic and the followers of Fikret Abdic, at one point during the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At several points, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So we have reached the ultimate answer which could have been given right away, but that doesn't matter. Mr. Donia, yesterday we agreed that in history it's happened frequently that a historical fact that was considered to be absolutely accurate later is established to be inaccurate or twisted and so on and so forth. So my question to you is: Is it possible that after a certain period of time has passed, the court or the judgement of history which you are working on, theoretically the court can base its decision on a fact that can later be proved as inaccurate or not quite true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're speaking of one fact, I think yes, it is possible that any body judging anything could mistake one fact at any point in time and later be -- have that demonstrated not to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to move to a different topic now. Mr. Donia, you don't need to be an expert historian for this but just somebody who watches television and reads the press regularly for this introductory part of my question. Did you have the opportunity while reading the papers and watching television to hear some well-known public figure, a politician or a figure from show business, music, sports, and so on, an artist denies their own statement that had been published in the press or on television by asserting that the statement was misconstrued by taking parts of the statement out of context and that such a distorted statement was given a completely different meaning than the one intended? Have you ever come across such things?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then probably you know the old journalistic rule that a denial never has the same range as the -- or impact as the initial piece of news?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of that old journalist rule? All right. I'm going to put it simply, but a denial would equal the attempt to pick up feathers that were thrown all around from the tenth floor. I'm just using this as an illustration to show what a denial is considered to be. I'm also going to say that a denial occurs after a certain period of time has passed. It's not topical anymore, and journalists being rogues can put that denying on the tenth page, for example, instead of on the front page. So analogous to this journalistic theory, in your science one major historical fact or an event, is it possible to take out specific incidents or occurrences using a specific methodology and then put these things together in order to form a particular picture or image?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you testified in several cases before this Tribunal. You testified by being issued a specific assignment by the Prosecution, which is quite normal, and then you would be provided with documents in order to reach your conclusion. Then you would be given an indictment with one or two accused, one or two municipalities, and then would you do your work on that basis. You would get the same thing in the second case, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, tenth case. Mr. Donia, by dealing with history in this matter, treating it bit by bit, would there be a danger of what we referred to earlier and that is to get a distorted picture of the whole event rather than what would be the result of looking at the event as a whole?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with your characterization of what I have been asked to do nor what I have done in response to the commissions I've received in the various cases. In a number of those cases I've been asked to do exactly that process that you just described, which is to place events alleged in the indictment in a much broader context as part of more general trends or developments within the region. So I guess I'd have to say I don't see that problem arising in at least some of the work that I've done in -- in previous cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you did not have the job in any cases before this to give a general context or overview that was not strictly related to a particular case. You were not tasked with providing a general overview of the -- of the events or to deal with the situation in general without this being related to some particular case. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without it being related to some particular case, yes, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, do you know what the principle et altera pars means? It's a shortened version of that saying, but do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's the principle which says that one always needs to listen to the other side first, and that is the principle on which the work of this Tribunal is also based, including the methodology of allowing both sides to put forward their views and theories. The Defence has the right to state their counter-arguments to your arguments according to that principle, that one needs to hear the other side too.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you is: Can it happen that a Defence, because they are lacking resources, time, or do not believe this historical context to be relevant, do not take that opportunity and that you present your views on the basis of what you yourself have and what the Prosecution has given to you in terms of material?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it happen that the Defence -- if I understand your question correctly, you're asking could it happen that a Defence would not be able to present a different history? Yes, it could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is just what I wanted to ask. Very well. Mr. Donia, I'm going to finish my introductory part that I indicated, and now I'm going to focus now on specific work of yours. Mr. Donia, it was not your task to make a concrete report for this case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You did make a number of reports, and we have concluded that the one that is the most general, which would be relevant for all the cases, including this one, from a historical context and not from a perspective of the guilt or innocence of our clients, this work is called "The Origins of Republika Srpska in the Period From 1990 to 1992." Do you have that work in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I do, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I -- Mr. Donia -- Dr. Donia wasn't given any copies of his own reports, just documents that he was going to refer to. So the answer is no, he hasn't, unless the Defence have got a copy for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution in possession of a copy that we can lend to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think our legal assistant has a copy that can be made available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think in future it would help if the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In future, if the Defence want a witness to have a copy of a statement or report, could they notify us and we'll have one in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia -- ah, here it is. Perhaps they do have a copy. Okay. Now you have a copy in front of you. Mr. Donia, since your work is not divided into paragraphs and so for the interpreters and the benefit of the Chamber, I'm going to refer to the pages in English and in B/C/S. So we are in the introductory part of the report, and that's on page 1 of both the B/C/S and the English, although in the English version it does go on to the next page. You are explaining the reasons for the break-up of the Yugoslav Federation, which consisted of six republics, as we all know, and the Republic of Serbia had two autonomous provinces too. The attempts by certain republics after the fall of Communism to secede is something that you defined in the first passage of your report as separatism. However, the attempts of the Serbian leadership, which, as you say, is led by Slobodan Milosevic, you define as hegemony. So my question is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told by Mr. Smith that the report is in e-court so that you can have a look at it if the Defence call it up. It's 65 ter 10001.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question that relates to this relationship between separatism and hegemony, you define the attempts to preserve Yugoslavia's hegemony. Does that mean that Abraham Lincoln who attempted to preserve the federation of the United States of America as hegemony when faced with the idea of the -- attempt to secede by the 13 states of the United States when they tried to preserve slavery in -- from 1861 to 1865?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see this document? I'm talking about the introductory part of the report, practically the first page. Can we please look at that on e-court, because I see that it has not been shown on e-court. This is on page 03082476. Yes. This is the cover page. Can we look at the next page, please. Can we turn to the next page, please. Very well. Yes. We can see it now, and we can follow both the Serbian and the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, have you heard my question? Do you remember what I asked?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question was would I describe Abraham Lincoln's efforts as hegemonic, and no, I would not. I would point out that I have taken these two words or concepts from Raif Dizdarevic who was president of the Yugoslav Presidency at the time, and he was describing two tendencies, one to strengthen or firm up the federation and the other to weaken it, and I wouldn't view Abraham Lincoln's efforts to strengthen the federal state of the United States but, rather, to maintain it. So the dichotomy that is positioned here by Mr. Dizdarevic, I wouldn't characterize -- extend that same characterization to Lincoln's efforts in the US.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to page 2 in B/C/S, and that's still page 2 English. In English it would be paragraph 2. The sub-heading is "The mobilisation of Serbian nationalism." Dr. Donia, I'll try to move through this section about the Yugoslav crisis more quickly, and please answer me with a yes or no. You quote here the words of Slobodan Milosevic, who says, "Nobody shall beat you." And that's in the context of Serbian nationalism. If you put this in the context of his entire speech, would it be an attempt to calm down the passions, the condemnation of Albanian nationalism and separatism and the condemnation of police violence against the Serbian people? Would it be a proper qualification of his -- of the tenor of his entire speech?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what -- I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can these words also mean an attempt to calm down the passions and the condemnation of police brutality against Serbian people down there in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context I don't see how that would be a possible interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I am talking about the broader context, but obviously we don't agree. Do you know when the tensions in Kosovo started? In other words, to the best of your knowledge, when did the first demonstrations of ethnic Albanians in Kosovo begin with the demand for Kosovo to become a republic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the quest for an independent Albanian state goes back to, say, the 1870s, and those demonstrations occurred periodically over the next hundred years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. On the same page you say further down: "Six months later, Milosevic was elected president of the League of Communists of Serbia, giving him undisputed control in Serbia." And this is a quotation from an author, Crnobrnja. Is that correct that's the last line in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, such a position in the League of Communists does not exist. That post does not exist, and Slobodan Milosevic, thus, did not hold it. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll move to page 3 in B/C/S, and I think we're already on page 3 English. Here you discuss demonstrations in Vojvodina. Do you know who led the protesters in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If I say that it's Mihajl Kertes, an ethnic Hungarian, was leading the protests, would it sound strange to you that it would be an ethnic Hungarian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would it sound strange that Kertes would lead those demonstrations? No, not at all. And his ethnicity would not be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If you say so. I can only say I don't agree, but let's move on. You mentioned that the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina learned of a plan that a grenade should be thrown into Cvijetin causing or disturbing the demonstration and provoking a police reaction. Where did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- this is in Raif Dizdarevic's book of memoirs, "Od smrti Tita do smrti Jugoslavije."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Concerning events in Montenegro, you say that again about these demonstrations you are describing, and we are now on page 4 in English, you say that 40 buses and a large number of passenger cars moved towards Montenegro to attend these demonstrations. Do you know from where these people set out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If I say that they set out from Niksic, a town in Montenegro, not Belgrade, would that mean something to you? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to move to page 5 of your report now, paragraph 1. Towards the end you say: "On the 28th of March, the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia adopted constitutional amendments that eliminated most of Kosovo's autonomy within the republic." Mr. Donia, do you know exactly what it was that the Assembly enacted that day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I pretty much said here what I know of those amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just present one fact and you tell me if I'm right. According to the then-constitution of Serbia, amendments could not happen without the consent of the two autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo. So these provincial assemblies practically had the right of veto and could block the process of amending the constitution. Now, this amendment only abolished their right of veto, not the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina which remained intact. You said you did not have detailed knowledge about this and you were not a constitutional expert, but we will invite one later and deal with the issue. Mr. Donia we're still on page 5. Here you deal with the nationalism of the Serbian and Montenegrin people, and you say: "By the spring of 1989, Serbian nationalism prevailed in the official government bodies of the republics of Serbia and Montenegro, and the Serbs outside these two republics were constantly still receiving messages of nationalist tenor."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel -- could counsel repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Which people live in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a question people argue about a lot. The ethnic composition, which I take it is what you are asking about, in most recent times is about evenly divided between those who identify themselves as Montenegrins by nationality and those who identify themselves as Serbs. There are also significant numbers of other peoples, principally Albanians but also Bosniaks and Roma and a few other minority peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Concerning protests in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you say that the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina prohibited the display of nationalist symbols. We're on page 6, paragraph 2, now. Would the display -- was the display of other ethnic symbols in Serbia prohibited, such as the display of Albanian symbols in Serbia, for instance, at rallies and gatherings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This ban I'm speaking of is -- was for the purpose of this demonstration. It was not a general ban on display of symbols of any nation or people. I don't think there were in Yugoslavia at that time any -- any such general bans on the display of those symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us go back for a moment it page 5. You claim that Mr. Milosevic invoked the rights of other ethnicities, and you say that that would become the most common goods.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel give a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, the interpretation is asking if you could guide them to the reference in the document where you are, which page and paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5, paragraph one, the last line. Sorry, second paragraph, the last line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: "And he urged toleration and respect for the rights for other nationalities, rhetoric that would become a staple in the lexicon of Serbian nationalism." What kind of staple are you talking about, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is that it became a standard, routine part of Serbian nationalist rhetoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Donia. We'll move back to page 6 in English. Let's see which paragraph it is. It's the third full paragraph. Here you talk about the Serbian Orthodox Church, which also spread the Serbian nationalist message by moving the earthly remains of Prince Lazar. Do you know what such relics are, and do you know that in Catholic temples the shroud that allegedly covered the body of Jesus Christ is preserved, and the spear that was held -- that was carried through the Crusades by Barbarossa, et cetera, do you consider that a symbol of nationalism, and do you consider the display of symbols of faith and traditional costumes, do you consider that to be the marking of territory? Let me give you a very blatant example. Here in the Netherlands we see a variety of traditional costumes. Would all the people wearing them marking their own territory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. I think you point out that the specific circumstances and context it makes all the difference in the, let's say, public -- the public theatre associated with the deployment of relics and -- and symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn to page 7 in English, paragraph one. Here you claim that the exhumed remains did not belong exclusively to Serbs. Would that mean that Catholic Croats and Muslims were also thrown into those pits?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement in the report is it was unclear, and I would hold to that. It wasn't clear to -- at the time that they were thrown in, necessarily, who those folks were and probably not clear at the time that they were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but then you contradict yourself in another paragraph where you say: "Local Serbs often knew of those corpses, and they remembered that those were Serbs who were victims of the Croat slaughter in the Second World War." So the local Serbs knew who those dead people were.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We're still on that page. You characterize those burials as pompous reburials. Would you then consider the throwing of those bodies, in the first place, a proper burial?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The word in English, by the way, is "ostentatious."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we followed this passage in English. It's a matter of interpretation. Further down the page, page 7, there's another interesting paragraph. You discuss the multi-party elections in various republics. Do you know who prevent the holding of Yugoslav multi-party elections into Yugoslav bodies? Not republic but Yugoslav bodies.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding was it was a combination of the Slovenes and Serbs who opposed that taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Where did this combination of Slovenes and Serbs take place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the discussions in the federal bodies, but I -- more specific I can't be than that. I just don't know the specific discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Then you would not agree that it was the Croat and Slovene separatists, although you deal in your report with the Croatian and Slovene separatists.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent of my knowledge, no. It was a combination of Slovene leaders and Serb leaders who opposed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Obviously we can only agree to disagree and we'll have to lead further evidence. Well -- we're on page 7 in English, paragraph four. There you say that the Assembly of Slovenia, in July 1990, made a key step towards independence by adopting the resolution proclaiming the sovereignty of Slovenia. Do you know that the Slovene Assembly actually adopted amendments to the existing Slovenian constitution establishing its independence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did indeed adopt amendments to the constitution at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, what do you know about the history of Slovene statehood? And my question more specifically would be: Was Slovenia ever a state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to 1991 it was not an independent state, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would it mean something to you if I said it has never been a state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you then agree with me that its external borders were the borders of Yugoslavia, not the borders of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Whereas its internal borders dividing it from other parts of Yugoslavia were administratively established after World War II in 1945.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "administratively established." If we characterize them as internal borders or boundaries, yes, they were established after World War II by the Tito regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Finally we agree on something. Mr. Donia, under the prevailing constitution at the time, was any change in the external borders by unilateral decisions of a republic or province prohibited, and therefore was this act of the Slovene Assembly contrary to the federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That leads me to an area that I'm not competent to answer in, as I'm not a constitutional lawyer nor specialist on constitution law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I asked you this because you deal quite a great deal in your report with constitution issues, but, however, one thing may be indisputable. Would you agree that the Yugoslav People's Army's job was to protect the territorial integrity, the unity of Yugoslavia and its external borders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you noted that in your report. I underlined that. Are you aware that unconstitutional change of external borders of Yugoslavia or secession was qualified in the Criminal Code as a serious crime?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a question of constitutional interpretation that I can't -- I'm not qualified to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on. Can you tell me what you know about the history of Croatian statehood? Had Croatia ever been a state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Tell us when?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From about 800 to -- it remained a state until 1102 at the very earliest, and certain elements of its statehood, specifically the diet, actually survived until 1918. It then became a state again in 1941 until 1945, or a state under the name of Croatia existed during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This statehood between 1941 and 1945 is something I'll deal with later. Let me ask you this: Studying the history of Yugoslav peoples, did you come to the conclusion that in both previous states of Yugoslavia Serbs invested their statehood and suffered the greatest losses in order to create that joint state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You would not agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know, Mr. Donia, that the Federal Constitutional Court proclaimed the Slovene amendments unconstitutional, and if you know that, why did you not write that in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I know it? Yes. There's actually a book that treats it by Bob Hayden. I generally didn't include in the report the Constitutional Court pronouncements on various acts, I think with perhaps one exception, mainly because I didn't find them of much consequence in the actual development or evolution of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We're still on the same passage. You deal with multi-party elections, including in Croatia. That's page 8, paragraph two. And you say: "Out of the total of 356 seats, 206 were won by Croatian nationalists, and out of the 24 Serb MPs, only 5 were from the national ticket, meaning the SDS." Is this quotation correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you would agree with the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the problem is that the pages that Mr. Cvijetic is referring to don't appear to be -- I've been having some difficulty in following which paragraph he's quoting in English. I think Dr. Donia's having the same. And I think Dr. Donia needs to be shown the actual quote in English, even though he does speak the language, if he's going to agree or disagree that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Donia found this piece of information very quickly that I referred to. I said it was in passage two on page 8. I cannot define it any more specifically than that. May I continue, Your Honours? And I'm going to try to be even more precise when I'm citing the passages in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the elections in Serbia and Montenegro, page 8, one-but-last paragraph. And you speak about the address by Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. Does it not seem to you, Mr. Donia, that you ascribed the election campaign address by another leader of a Serbian party, the Serbian Renewal Movement, Vuk Draskovic, with that of Slobodan Milosevic? I can remind you of what Vuk Draskovic said. He used extreme nationalist rhetoric claiming that: "The Serbian borders lay where the Serbian graves lie."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: "And his calm rhetoric has contributed to his victory in those elections." In other words, in December 1990, in Milosevic's public addresses there was not any trace of nationalism. Do you agree with my assertion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Donia, is the data correct that only in Serbia and Montenegro the victories were not claimed by parties with a nationalist or ethnic tone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some local areas in which non-nationalist parties prevail even in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in -- in other republics as well, and the victories of the nationalists were -- they were not uniform across the other republics of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, can we move on? Page 9, paragraph three, last line. My question is: Did you have the Constitution of Serbia of the 28th of September, 1990, in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then I cannot ask you about -- or perhaps I can ask you. How do you draw the conclusion that you draw in this last line?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you've -- as you can see, I have footnoted and quoted Robert Hayden who has studied that constitution and the whole question of constitutional law. He's an attorney and an anthropologist of law. I've relied on him for this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So this is not your conclusion then.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my conclusion based on his study of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I am going to put the opposite assertion to you, that these changes did not abolish the autonomy of Kosovo or Vojvodina, but they actually kept the autonomy that they had under previous constitutions from 1973 [as interpreted] and also 1969.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's wrong. The autonomy that Kosovo and Vojvodina was firmly established in the 1974 Constitution, and taken away, withdrawn in the constitutional amendments and ultimately the changes that we're talking about in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would just like to ask for a correction to the transcript. I had said 1963, not 1973.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us continue, Mr. Donia. On page -- let me just find the English version. Page 10, paragraph three, you deal with the addresses of Mr. Jovan Raskovic. We all know this was a Serb who was leading the Serbs in Croatia. Is that correct? And you assert that in spite of the insightful rhetoric, he limited his demands to cultural autonomy for the Serbs of Croatia and resolutely opposed territorial separatism. So I need to ask you whether this conclusion is opposite to the footnote on page 39 where Mr. Raskovic literally says: "We are not going to be creating another Serbian state in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. This is being imputed to us. We do not want to have a Serbia in Croatia. We just want the autonomy and sovereignty of a Serbian ethnic identity." Mr. Donia, do you know what the word "sovereignty" means? That's the specific question.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer one question at a time, if I may. Your question was: Is there a contradiction? And my answer is no. There -- I don't see a contradiction between what you just quoted from page 39 and the statement that Raskovic favoured a cultural autonomy. That was a consistent position of his, albeit stated with a great flourish and a great deal of rhetoric. And I -- to my knowledge, it never changed. As to the question of what "sovereignty" means, I think "sovereignty" means different things to different people, and I couldn't give you the dictionary definition the world, but it clearly assigns to a polity a primary position in decision-making about at least some of its own policy matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that the word was first used by Jean Bodin in his work six books about state, and this is where he gives the first definition of that word? All right. If you're not aware of that, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. All right. We're now on page 11, paragraph four. You assert here that Milosevic and Borisav Jovic agreed about the proposal to expel Slovenia and Croatia from the Yugoslav Federation. You also quote from Jovic's diary, but when you read the diary itself, you can see that only the -- this has to do -- that only members of the Presidency of Croatia and Slovenia be excluded from ruling on a specific issue, not that Slovenia and Croatia be expelled. Do you see the difference between those two things?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly see the difference. I would have to go back to the diary to see if that is the exact point that -- that was being made there. I'm sorry, I don't have the B/C/S in front of me, so I couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let us move to page 14, paragraph two, please. You deal with conflicts in Borovo Selo, that incident which you claim was caused by the men of Mr. Vojislav Seselj. Mr. Donia, the proceedings against Mr. Seselj are underway and there is a war being waged in the courtroom in relation to whether this is true or not. Don't you think that it is too early for you to be drawing conclusions on a case that is still underway? And you are also citing different sources. Are they reliable enough for you to be able to reach the conclusion that you reach?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's two questions at least. I was -- when I wrote these words, I don't believe Mr. Seselj was in the midst of a court proceeding. In fact, I believe he was not in -- not in the custody of the ICTY. So I would only say the disposition of that matter in the court would be of -- of value and interest in determining the full true story of -- or more complete story of what happened in -- in Borovo Selo. The account that I've given is based in part on the journalist's viewing of Belgrade television account of the event, and I would try to avoid the very controversial allegations that have arisen surrounding Borovo Selo and simply stick to the fundamental basic facts of what happened as it was reported at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, since you say that you're not an expert on constitutional matters, then on page 14, this conclusion of yours that Milosevic and Bulatovic were in favour of strengthening the current constitutional order, I wanted to ask you, did you look at constitutional projects from that period? You said you did not, so I'm going to abandon that question and move to page 14, paragraph five now. You interpret here the conversations between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic in Karadjordjevic, and you also quote Mr. Milic on this. It says: "Mr. Milic, do you know that those are minutes of those talks?"

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In order to make a serious historical conclusion on this, would it be a useful exercise to study those minutes, do you think?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We're now on page 16, paragraph three. Page 16, paragraphs two and three. You quote the words of Stipe Mesic here where he complains that immediately after the elections for the president of the Presidency and until the end, no one from the military leadership came to see him when he was the president of the Presidency. Do you know why this was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I answered that question in the next sentence here and quoting General Kadijevic who said, "We deliberately treated him that way."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mesic did not represent a direction that the JNA Supreme Command or high command wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, can this be linked with his statement that he was going to be the last president of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the Yugoslav People's Army was entrusted with preserving that state, that Yugoslavia. Is that perhaps the cause of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now that we're on the topic of Mr. Mesic, do you know anything about his statements about transferring the war from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, that he openly announced that Croatia intended to transfer the war from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to unburden or to lift the burden on the Croatian fronts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that statement of his. Do you know anything about the involvement of Croatia in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina through the direct participation of the Croatian armed forces and assistance in manpower and weapons to the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would we agree, and you wrote that in your report, that the first major war crime against the civilian population took place in the village of Sijekovac, and it was committed by Croatian forces who killed civilians in that Serbian village?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I wrote. I did report on -- in my paper on the attack on Sijekovac, but I also, at least if not this report, elsewhere reported on the attack on the village of -- in Herzegovina in October of 1991 by the JNA. I'm sorry, I'm forgetting the name of the village. Ravno. Which I viewed as the first serious armed incursion against civilians in Bosnia-Herzegovina from outside the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just going to remind you that I took this from your testimony in the Brdjanin case, and it was in response to a question by my learned friend Mr. Ackerman. The Trial Chamber can confirm that. In any case, it's about an awful -- an awful crime which was widely reported on television, and there is a lot of footage about that. So I guess we would agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If this was from the Brdjanin testimony, could we have the reference, please, to the page number and the day of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can provide that later. Since I don't know English, I'm listening to the transcripts from Mr. Donia's testimony, so I wrote the transcript references, and we can confirm that later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate in a Mr. Cvijetic doesn't read, speak English, but others on his team do, and if assertions are going to be made to a witness, it's important that we have the context in the sense of where we can find it so that we can check it's an accurate representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will easily clarify this with Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Donia, that a major war crime was committed in the village of Sijekovac against Serb civilians by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That is my final question there. Mr. Donia, I'm now going to move to page 17 of your report, and you have a heading there, "The Bosnian Context." Does that imply, Mr. Donia, that that is also the Herzegovinian context?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You cover the formation of the party established by the then-prime minister Mr. Ante Markovic, and that he decided to form the party at Kozara; is that correct? This is page 19, paragraph two. And you place that in the context of major sacrifices that were made in that area. So before that I would like to ask you when did Mr. Markovic form that party in relation to the elections in Croatia? Was it before the elections or after?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was founded after the elections in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with my assertion that Mr. Ante Markovic wanted to avoid or did not wish to interfere with Mr. Tudjman's victory in Croatia and wanted to rally the Croatian voter base in Bosnia in order to assure a victory for them there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know. I don't have the information to agree or disagree with your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Donia, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's time for a break now, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before we do break --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- can I just remind again Mr. Cvijetic of guideline 17: "The parties are to avoid paraphrasing previous testimony or statements of witnesses but shall quote the directly relevant passage and indicate the exact page numbers and relevant lines."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I withdrew that question. I rephrased it, and you realised that the whole matter was corrected; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we take the adjournment, I just wish to remind counsel that Dr. Donia, because of his previous commitments, that you would only have an hour with him when we return at quarter -- quarter of 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before we begin, I would kindly ask the Registrar could check how much time I've already spent out of my total allocated time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have spent one hour and 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday and today together, which means that for this cross-examination I have how much time left? Two hours and 30 minutes; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't think that a final ruling has been made on the extent of time for this, because we knew that we wouldn't complete today anyway, but we said yesterday that it would be somewhere between three and four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be very grateful if you would give me an indication, because today I cannot finish at any rate, and when Mr. Donia is recalled, I would like to know how much time I would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You will be given our ruling as soon as possible, but I suggest that we spend the time now in getting as far as we can with Dr. Donia, and then when Dr. Donia has left this morning, we still have some time for procedural matters, and we'll get back to it by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So hurry up and get on with the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I would like to move to page 20 -- 21, 21 in English. Last paragraph. This is about the decision of the Constitutional Court which judged that the Serbian National Council is an illegal body usurping the constitutional authority of the constitutional government. Mr. Donia, you dealt with this issue, and from the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the council of peoples was abolished. That exists in many multi-ethnic communities. There is a council in which all the various ethnicities are equally represented, and the mechanism of voting prevents out-voting in matters of vital national interest. You deal with this and you say that this body after that date did, in fact, no longer exist. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you misinterpreted what I wrote here. I wrote that the Constitutional Court ruled the Serbian National Council, which was this body that was proclaimed by Karadzic on October 13, 1990, as a purely Serbian body to be unconstitutional, and then that it referred the issue to the -- or to the Bosnian Assembly for further action, and this self-proclaimed or Karadzic-proclaimed body really never really functioned in Bosnia, whereas its counterpart in Serbia did. I wasn't speaking here about the actual Chamber of Peoples of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina but, rather, this body that was proclaimed by Karadzic and never really -- there was never any life breathed into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Correct. And I asked you only in that context, because you did deal with the issue of the absence of the Chamber of Peoples from the Bosnian Assembly in your report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question? What is your specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question was the existence of such a chamber in multi-ethnic communities, in parliaments, is something quite usual, especially when vital national interests and issues of vital national interests are voted on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frequent but I don't know that it's the norm for multi-ethnic societies. I just really don't know how many societies that you would call multi-ethnic actually have such a Chamber of Peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you will admit that the existence of such a chamber ensures a solid mechanism for protecting the vital national interest of each people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can function that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll deal briefly with page 22, paragraph two. This is the time of elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, mainly nationalist parties took part; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you reading a passage? I'm not finding --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm -- this is just an introductory remark, an introduction to a question that will have to do with paragraph two on page 22. Three nationalist parties appeared.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than that. There were total of, I think, 62 parties, of which many were nationalist in orientation and a good number were either non-nationalist or anti-nationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But nationalist parties were predominant.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the outcome of the election that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At those multi-party elections people also voted for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Presidency consisted of two representatives of each people, and there was a possibility for electing one member of the category called "Others"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now let's go back to paragraph two on page 22. You mention Ejup Ganic, who entered the Presidency as a representative of this category "Others." My question is how did he declare himself in terms of ethnicity at those elections?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't declare himself by ethnicity for the election. He entered as a candidate in the category of "Other" on the grounds that he had declared himself a Yugoslav in 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that's the point of my question. He declared himself as a Yugoslav. Do you know how Ejup Ganic declared himself during the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume he declared himself as a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Bosniak Muslim. At that time, in fact, it was Muslim, because the category of Bosniak had not yet been introduced.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the category of "Bosniak" was formally adopted by the Bosnian Muslims in September of 1993, so when I say "Bosniak," I'm really saying the same thing as Bosnian Muslim prior to September 1993. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, how, then, do you interpret the fact that somebody who declared himself as a Yugoslav and comes into the category of "Other" goes back into the category of "Muslim" during the war? Does that mean that he originally lied about his identity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He declared himself, as many people did, in the census of 1990 -- 1981 as a Yugoslav, and from 1981 to 1991, if you look at those census results, the number of people who declared themselves as Yugoslavs declined considerably. People, in other words, shifted their sense of identity, their national identity, and there is no reason to believe that he was lying in 1981 anymore than those other people were who underwent a shift of identity in their own feelings. I tried to make that point in the paper that I had written for the Karadzic case that this is a -- national identity is, in fact, a contingent element. So my answer to your question is, no, I don't believe he lied.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I suppose you wouldn't agree, then, with my theory that it was an election swindle. Mr. Ganic changed this identity very quickly. He enters the Presidency as a representative of "Others" and then soon thereafter declares himself as a Muslim and enters the SDA party. You wouldn't agree, would you, that he deceived the electorate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct, I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The law on political parties of 1990 allowed multi-party organisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina after a long period of one-party rule; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That law prohibited the establishment of parties with nationalist platforms and symbols that would rally only members of one people; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was -- sorry. Do you know that the Constitutional Court declared -- do you know that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared that law unconstitutional?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that's quite a correct characterization of the court's decision, but the effect of their ruling was to give a green light to the organisation of parties based on religious and national grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who was the -- the president of the Constitutional Court?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kasim Trnka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kasim Trnka later become a prominent member of the SDA party, Izetbegovic's party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, at presidential elections where members of the Presidency were to be elected, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic did not win the greatest number of votes, did he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What about Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He won -- he won the most votes in -- overall, and in the category, obviously, of "Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that Alija Izetbegovic became president of the Presidency rather than Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified yesterday, formally Izetbegovic was selected by a vote of all members of the Presidency. Prior to that vote, the three national parties reached an agreement which resulted in him being elected president, and the SDA itself elected -- or selected Izetbegovic to be the SDA's candidate for the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with my idea that Fikret Abdic conceded this position under serious threats by other members of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you agree with the theory that the course of historical events in Bosnia and Herzegovina would have been entirely different had Fikret Abdic been member -- been president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you answer in the affirmative to the same question when testifying previously in a different case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't -- I don't recall having answered that question previously, but it -- I'd have to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will not insist any further until I'm able to provide a reference for your testimony in the Brdjanin case, and then I will come back to it. Mr. Donia, you continue to discuss regionalisation. That's page 21, paragraph two. The first full paragraph, in fact. Can you see this? It's 23 in English, actually, and the sub-heading is "Regionalisation." Twenty-three. Can you see it now? May I continue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that inter-municipal co-operation and association was something that was allowed by the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is it true that both Croats and Muslims had their own versions of regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were -- there were regional associations established and in existence in 1990, but they were not ethnic or national in composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the sake of expediency, I will go through Mr. Donia's report and tender certain things into evidence later, or perhaps I should tender 1D003801 -- 3810. 1D003810.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what is that exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's one document of the SDA party on the establishment of a separate municipality within Banja Luka, populated mainly by Muslims. I don't know if you -- if this document has been called up. It's in e-court. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, just a moment. I -- we were given yesterday a bundle of documents from the Defence, but I don't see one that's 1D003810.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know it's in e-court because it was on the screen a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I've spotted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? That is the document. It's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My affection for e-court grows by the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There are other electronic dinosaurs. You're not the only one. So you see the document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see the document, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Does it confirm what you said a moment ago, that there were instances of regional organisation on all sides?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said a moment ago. I said there were regional associations in existence that had been created in the 1970s and before that were in existence in 1990 but were not national or ethnic in character. The document that you're showing me validates what I've known about for some time and is referred to in many other documents, which was this rather fleeting attempt of the SDA to form a separate municipality within Banja Luka. I believe there was also an effort to establish one in the Sarajevo area. There were a few isolated instances of forming separate municipalities by -- by Muslims. But this was not regionalisation. This was a different phenomenon than you asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I will lead evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this now as a Defence exhibit? Our number is D13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I'll show you another document for -- 1D002854. It's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We see that this is about Herzegovina Regional Community and the Travnik Regional Community under the Croatian Democratic Union. Do you know about the existence of this regional community? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What is of interest to me here are the dates. The previous document was September 1991, and this one is dated 12 December -- 12 November 1991. So these are not the old regional communities. These are some new regional communities.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was part of several associations of municipalities that were proclaimed -- I thought it was the 9th of November, 1991, by Mate Boban and the separatist wing of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and clearly under the influence of Franjo Tudjman and the Zagreb leadership of the HDZ. I've written about this in previous reports for other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Donia. You've just answered -- you've just anticipated my next question. There were communities established based on the national criterion; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were communities established by Serbs and Croats on the national basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Aren't you mistaken? I showed you two documents, one about a Muslim regional community and another about a Croat regional community.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have missed it, but I saw nothing in the document that you showed me suggesting a Muslim regional community of municipalities, which is -- but then what you -- you've been asking me about. The document referred only to the -- as I -- as I recall -- or what I saw, referred to the proclamation of a separate municipality, Banja Luka-Stari Grad, and not an association of municipalities as a regional phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask a clarifying question, because I think you mentioned that this was attempted in Banja Luka and also in Sarajevo. And so my question would be: Did any of those attempts actually succeed? Were any Muslim municipalities ever created in either Banja Luka or Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither of those ever came to life in any significant way. The one that did ultimately was formed and had actually a significant role was the Western Bosnia association around Bihac, which was headed by Fikret Abdic. That was created some months later than the -- after the war was -- was already underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I tender the previous document as a Defence exhibit. Sorry, this document we are discussing now. I'm already holding the next one, and I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, it may be tendered and admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could I please have the document ID or the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D002854.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It has, actually, a different number on the bottom. It says 2856.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 54 is what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 1D2, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, since you've touched upon the issue of Sarajevo, I'd like to tender -- to introduce another document, 1D002778. I think we have it on the screen now. What's interesting about this document and why I'd like to tender it later is the final part, the paragraph 4 on page 2. Could we turn to page 2. Paragraph 4. It's the SDA party, the Democratic Action Party, invoking the constitutional provision about regionalisation. You have already spoken about Sarajevo. I'd just like to tender this as another Defence exhibit. 1D002778.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, it maybe admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: 1D003828 is another document in support of this. Mr. Donia, can you see the document now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not well, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's the statutory decision on the organisation of a Stari Grad-Banja Luka Municipal Assembly in the process of establishment. This is a follow-up on the previous decision. Now we have a statutory decision. Since you've already commented, I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D4, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the date on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: 17 November 1991. Correct? Do you agree that this is in fact an implementation, a step toward implementing the previous decision?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I could just note, it says "Illegible" on the English. I don't see anything illegible about the date on the B/C/S. It's clearly 11th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: 17 November; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And yes, I agree it is a -- implementing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I tender this document as well or has it been admitted already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It already has been.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll now show you a very interesting document, 1D003749. Mr. Donia, do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's quite a curious document in which all the participating parties in Banja Luka municipality issue a proclamation regionalising that area. Serbs, Croats, and Muslims alike regionalise the area and write this whole study. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't accept your characterization of it until I've read it and seen specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you're asking me to agree, I need to be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I'm done with the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we tender this document, 1D00 -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I don't accept your characterization of the document. This is not regionalisation as it was defined and applied by the SDS. This is simply the division of one municipality into several. It's a different process than what you are referring to as regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We don't have to agree, Mr. Donia. I can call this document joint Variants A and B agreed upon by Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Cvijetic. I'm not sure about what this document is supposed to show. What is it that you want to bring to the Court's attention with this document? I don't have page 1 on the screen anymore so I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This offsets the assertion of the Prosecution that the SDS, with its A and B variants, divided municipalities based on the majority population. Now we see a similar decision agreed upon by all the parties in that region, and this is what the document confirms, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But is it an invitation to sign up between the different parties for purposes of an election or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This applies only to the territories of the municipalities listed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. I see on the bottom of page 1 that: "The inhabitants of all local communes, settlements and villages are called upon at meetings to vote for the foundation of each their municipalities because by," and then it turns over to page 2, "voting in favour they will be voting for the prosperity of their neighbourhood and a harmonious social and economic development overall."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it assists -- if it assists, we're not objecting to it. We don't think it's got anything to do Variant -- any type of Variant A and B. It seems to be a community of municipalities, rather likely, but we're quite happy to have it admitted if the Defence want it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Chamber has no objections to admitting it, it's just that we want to be sure that we understand what the document is purporting to bring.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To put it briefly, Your Honour, this is an agreement between parties that preceded the later -- the subsequent statutory decision already admitted concerning Stari Grad-Banja Luka. This decision was made based on an agreement among parties. That's 1D003749.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll let it in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D5, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say it doesn't seem to appear on transcript that I said we don't think it's got anything to do with Variant A or B, on line 18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I respond to the question that I was asked earlier about this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, you've mischaracterized the document. It is a draft of an agreement. It is not signed. And it was very common practice in these Assembly meetings to -- for someone to arrive at a meeting with a draft just like this and ask that it be approved by everyone present. Common practice pretty much in any city council or so. But there are no signatures or stamps on the document that indicate that it's been approved by these parties. I would assess it as highly unlikely that the SDS in particular would -- would agree with this document, and in fact the SDS's name isn't even listed there. And I think the other parties would be unlike to -- unlikely to approve it as well. And I just -- in the absence of signatures, very much doubt that it represents an agreement that was actually reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, can you clarify? Was this document ever adopted?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an inference we are draw based on the fact that this was followed by the statutory decision proclaiming municipalities. That's how we draw the inference, and we found this document among the disclosed material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
