utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. My question was whether this document had been adopted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We suppose that it was, because it says the analysis is adopted in full, and then this was followed by that statutory decision. So we infer, we conclude, that it must have been. This was also followed by an identical decision of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the first [indiscernible], can I say we'd ask for those documents to -- counsel's just giving evidence at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was answering your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps in response to the observation that Ms. Korner has made I should indicate the Chamber's view as to this document, Counsel, that it is -- bearing in mind that you are not entitled to give evidence, it is the witness who is giving the evidence, that the document, although we have admitted it, that having regard to the arguments that -- that in effect you're advancing, that is something that we would have to revisit at the appropriate stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I just ask. I'm not clear from that. Is Your Honour ruling that they must provide the documents that Mr. Cvijetic has referred to? Because that's what we're asking for, because Mr. Cvijetic has just made certain assertions. I'm simply inquiring whether Your Honour has made the ruling that the Defence must provide us with the documents that Mr. Cvijetic says surround these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you repeat the question that you had posed to the Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. Your Honour, my -- you referred to my objection, and I simply objected that Mr. Cvijetic was giving evidence and that we would like to see the documents that he referred to, namely, the decisions that followed he asserted, before this went any further, and I was asking whether Your Honour was ruling that the Defence must provide us with those documents rather than Mr. Cvijetic telling the Chamber that they exist, that that was -- I was merely asking will Your Honour rule that the Defence, if they wish this document to be taken any further, should provide us with copies of the other documents. That -- that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we have to formally rule on that at that stage. You made an objection which -- and I characterize it as an observation but obviously it was an objection, and that is where matters stand. If counsel seeks to take the Chamber where he has indicated he expects that he could be having regard to how he has characterized that document, then obviously he would have to lead the relevant evidence, but I don't think it is necessary for the Chamber to rule at this stage that he must provide the supporting evidence. It would be up to him if he intends to rely on it to that extent, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this must be a misunderstanding. Before this document, both the documents I'm referring to were admitted, 1D0038 -- in fact, they were called 1D1 and 1D4, and the document I'm tendering now precedes them. I suppose I don't have to provide a rationale for something that's already been admitted into evidence. The admitted documents are a result of the one I'm holding in my hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We accept the logic of that, and perhaps I didn't explain our view sufficiently clearly. What we are saying is that, as you have just correctly indicated, that having regard to the connection between this document and the previously tendered documents, notwithstanding any technical objection that could have been taken that it should only have been marked for identification, we have allowed it as an exhibit, and that is as far as we are going at this stage. The rest of it are matters for argument at the appropriate stage. Does that clarify? Does that address your concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and I think that is in keeping with paragraph 4 of your guidelines. But I would like to move on. That's document 1D003691.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can we agree - I'm going to paraphrase the text - that a group of citizens of the Neum inhabited place is asking for instructions from the democratic party -- Democratic Action Party from Sarajevo, that they are under pressure from Croats, that Muslim children have to obtain textbooks from Croatia and study from those textbooks. And I'm speaking about this as proof of the functioning of another large community, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was founded in November of 1991 and this document is dated September of 1991, that is a highly unlikely relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we are going to come back to the formation of Herceg-Bosna, but I think Their Honours are looking at the clock. Perhaps I can just ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I continue? Do I have time to continue? The Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna is a separate topic that I will be dealing with. So obviously I'm running out of time. Perhaps it would be better for me not to even begin. I don't know if you agree request that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Donia can be here to 12.00 if it assists. That will enable him to get his flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you finish this up in 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, then it's basically up to you whether you wish to begin. You may decide that you would rather stop now and then resume with the next item that you wish when Dr. Donia comes back, or you may wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting, but I would just like to ask for this document to be admitted. We have just enough time for that. 1D00369, perhaps we could ask for this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, but admitted on what basis? Dr. Donia doesn't say he's seen the document, doesn't agree with the proposition that's been put about it, so on what basis is it being admitted? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I heard Dr. Donia properly, he did state his position on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I must admit, Mr. Cvijetic, that I, too, have a bit of difficulty in fully understanding what it is that this document is supposed to show. There's a mother complaining that her kids have been forced to buy Croatian schoolbooks and that they were Muslim and that she had already bought those books, and the only comment that Dr. Donia provided was that this event occurred before the creation of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So with this information, then what do you want the Chamber to understand from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is precisely why I asked to stop here and to deal with Herceg-Bosnia separately, because the day and the time that Herceg-Bosnia was formed I'm going to provide a lot of documents indicating that it existed and that it was formed much earlier. That is the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Cvijetic, I would suggest that you tender the document when we have completed that exercise, and then we will take a position on whether or not to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. Then I can complete that and admit this document with other documents. Of course I accept your suggestion. Thank you. Your Honours, we were just talking about the possibility of ending the cross-examination as I am just about to deal with two key topics of my cross-examination for which I will be needing the time remaining to me, and none of those topics that I wish to deal with can be dealt with properly in ten minutes. So if you would permit me, I would like to continue next time to cover two what I consider crucial topics for which I will be needing the time that is left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the interpretation came through to us. Are you able to do this in ten minutes or would you rather wait?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to put it off, because I cannot even begin properly in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Was there something else, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can just help perhaps to make your decision easier. My colleague is suggesting that the document must be marked for identification at least, and the Registry probably agrees with that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document -- sorry. The document will be dealt with at a later stage. At this point, in the Chamber's view it's premature to even mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with your decision, Your Honours. I can just give you a promise. You said that Mr. Donia, next time, will be cross-examined on the three chapters of his most recent report, and we were permitted an hour and a half, if I am not mistaken. We are going to cut short our cross-examination time on those three chapters and then this part of mine that I still have to complete will fit in with that total hour and a half, perhaps requiring an additional half an hour or so. So we're not going to take up more than two hours in all for all of those matters for cross-examination. So I promise we will not need more than two hours to finish, and I think that is about how much time I have left anyway when we deduct the time that was spent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, as would have been indicated to you, you will have to return for the completion of your cross-examination. We thank you for your attendance today, and you may now withdraw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention one matter, and that's this: Transport for Dr. Donia. I understand we have had an e-mail from VWS. Perhaps, Dr. Donia, just wait a moment. That they don't arrange transport to and from the airport for expert witnesses. They will do it for non-experts but not for experts. We are perfectly prepared to have an investigator from our team drive Dr. Donia to -- no. Well, he says no. All right. I couldn't speak to Dr. Donia, obviously. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exactly. Because we should remind you that you are not allowed to have any contact with this Prosecution team during your absence from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Now, as we indicated yesterday, there are a number of the matters which must be addressed with the assistance for counsel, so it is proposed that we take a 20-minute break at this point, returning at 12.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do I understand Your Honours are going to raise some matters? If so, perhaps we could know before the adjournment so that if we need any paperwork we can bring it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There are a couple of rulings we need to make still, one of which is when should Donia come back, how much time does the Defence have -- the Stanisic Defence have left. That has not been decided. How much time does Zupljanin's Defence team wish to use? And then I think there are still a couple of issues relating to some of the motions that were filed recently that still haven't been ruled upon. So I think there are five or six small matters that need to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Because, Your Honours, we are certain, as we said yesterday, going to deal orally with our response to the application to appeal in respect of Dr. Nielsen, and then we've got a couple of matters, really administrative matters, including the question of Dr. Donia's ability to talk to other members of this office, because he's coming back to testify, I believe it's the end of October, and obviously those members of our office need to be able to speak to him about that testimony, so we need a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. We have actually discussed that, and we will hand down our ruling, but you will see that in my instructions to Dr. Donia I told him that he was not allowed to talk to any members of this team.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We apologise for keeping the parties and counsel waiting. The -- I would now invite Judge Harhoff to deal with the several matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We have considered a number of procedural matters which we will now address. The first issue is the time that the Defence teams have left for the cross-examination of Dr. Donia, and the Chamber originally indicated that -- and that was upon the suggestions made by the Stanisic team, that it would be somewhere between three and four hours of cross-examination. The Chamber has therefore decided that it will grant all together three and a half hours for the cross-examination of Stanisic, and that includes the cross-examination on the Sarajevo report. The Stanisic Defence team, as we understand, has so far taken 2 hours and 17 minutes this leaves 1 hour and 13 minutes to add up to the total time of three and a half hours. So Mr. Cvijetic, when Dr. Donia comes back you have 1 hour and 13 minutes to complete your cross-examination. As for the Zupljanin Defence team, we have been guided by Mr. Pantelic's own admission that in large part the Sarajevo report would not be of any particular relevance and that Mr. Pantelic would need either one hour or one and a half hours. The Chamber has granted you one hour. This means altogether that when Dr. Donia comes back, the Stanisic Defence team will continue and have 1 hour and 13 minutes, after which the Zupljanin Defence team will have one hour, and then there will be questions perhaps in redirect from the Prosecution and possibly by the Chamber, and that will then conclude the testimony of Dr. Donia. That's the first decision or order that we have rendered. The next ruling was concerned with the time for Dr. Donia's return to testify. The Chamber suggests that he be called to reappear before this Chamber at the time when he is coming back to The Hague anyway, and we understood that to be by the end of October. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- the order that we have issued is that Dr. Donia is to reappear upon his next visit to The Hague in, we understood, late October. So you can have him call and reappear either here before or after his testimony in those other cases in which he is involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just mention I checked with the lawyer involved. He will either be testifying in the last week of October or the first week of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, but whatever then we -- that is the time when we wish to see him so as to minimise the travel costs and the trouble for the witness himself. The third order we wish to render is a formalisation of what I think has already been indicated, but the Chamber's ruling is that Dr. Donia is not allowed to have any contact with your team and vice versa. Nobody from your team is allowed to have any contact with Dr. Donia. And it goes without saying that other members of the Prosecution with whom Dr. Donia will be having contact in relation to his testimony in other cases are not allowed, of course, to address any issue relevant to this case. The fourth motion -- the fourth issue, sorry, that we wish to address is the question of Dr. Nielsen's expert status, and we will reserve our ruling on this matter in view of the submissions made by Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, concerning that issue, I was prepared to make an oral submission in term of the Prosecution's response if you were willing to hear that today rather than filing something in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We certainly always prefer the most expedient and adequate ways. As I said, we have -- we will defer our decision on the matter and hand down a written decision, and we would be happy to hear your submissions when I have completed my order of rulings. May I, in relation to Nielsen, also add that in light of the difficulties that have occurred in relation to translation of the documents which the Defence wishes to confront Mr. Nielsen with, the Chamber strongly advises that Dr. Nielsen or -- be called at a time when the translation issue has been settled, because we think that it is inconvenient to first have him examined-in-chief and then wait for a long time until the translation issues have been solved in November, only then to have him reappear for cross-examination. So we have discussed whether we should hand down a straightforward order to defer the testimony of Dr. Nielsen until such time as the translation has been issued, or whether we should recommend this in very, very strong terms, and a majority in the Chamber found that it would perhaps be crossing over the lines that must exist between the Prosecution and the Chamber and the division between judicial powers and prosecutorial powers. So we thought it might be perhaps somewhat inappropriate to hand down a straightforward order. But if you can read what I'm saying between the lines, what the Chamber really wants to say is that we shouldn't hear Dr. Nielsen until such time as we have all the documents ready so that we can have him come and testify in chief and cross at the same time. The fifth --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I -- may I, Judge Harhoff, come in on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can we just wait until --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- we have -- because you understand we're coming back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- Dr. Nielsen, so let's just keep it all together. The fifth matter that we discussed was the suggestion that was made at the Pre-Trial Conference of postponing witnesses to whom the late filings related for a period of two months running from the Pre-Trial Conference. I think it was on the 3rd of September. This proposal was made and was intended to have a punitive character because we were disturbed by the late disclosure of the Prosecution. So in light of the fact that the intention and the purpose of the two months' delay was not only practical purposes but also had a touch of indicating to the Prosecution this time that we are serious about the time limits that are set out and we're not prepared to accept or tolerate nonobservance of these time limits. In light of this, the order that we now render is the following: That the late-filed documents cannot be used before expiration of a two-month period running from the Pre-Trial Conference on 3rd of September, and that the witnesses to whom these documents relate equally and therefore cannot be called. Now, the Prosecution has filed a motion asking for exemptions to be made in relation to two of these witnesses, goes for ST 019 and ST 171. The Chamber has considered the situation in relation to these two witnesses and we understand that the Defence teams do not have any objections to raise about calling 019 at an earlier time but that they do have objections in relation to 171. The Chamber has therefore ruled that we will accept that we can -- that the Prosecution can call 019 prior to the expiration of the two-month period that runs from September 3rd until November 3rd, whereas the other witness, 171, shall have to wait until that time. These were the rulings that this Chamber wishes to make at this moment. Now I would invite Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before I give the floor to Mr. Hannis, I would like to add, and excuse me for forgetting this additional part of the last order, namely, that for the other witnesses that fall into the category of having to wait ask, if the Prosecution can bring it up with the Defence teams and if the Defence teams will have no objections to calling any of those witnesses prior to the expiration of the two-month period, then that's fine with the Chamber, but if any of the Defence teams have any objections, then the order stands. Now, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Regarding Dr. Nielsen, the first thing I had wanted to address was the Defence motion for certification for leave to appeal your decision regarding his expert status, and in order to save time because we tentatively had him to be scheduled to be our first witness on the 29th of September, but I will address that in light of your remarks just now when I conclude this issue. We want to make an oral response to that request for certification. It's our position, Your Honours, that that request should be denied. As you know, under Rule 73(B), it's a two-prong test, first that the decision should involve an issue that significantly affects the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial; and secondly, that an immediate resolution of the issue may, in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, materially advance the proceedings. It's our position, Your Honour, that the Defence meet neither of the two prongs; and even if they did, we suggest that you should exercise your discretion to deny the motion. And we don't think it would have an impact on the evidence in the case. Any concerns regarding Mr. Nielsen we think can be addressed in deciding what weight to give his evidence at the end of the case, and we think that's the best way to address it and we would ask you therefore to deny the motion. With that -- and then I want to move on to the point you raised with the suggestion or recommendation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I don't know, could I ask you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- address the objection that is raised in Mr. Zecevic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Concerning his expertise or his closeness with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we would indicate that we think his expertise is set forth in his CV, which is part of the package. In addition, he has been allowed to testify as an expert in this Tribunal in other cases. He was an expert witness in the Krajisnik case, and he has also been admitted as an expert witness and his report received as an expert report in the pending case of Stanisic and Simatovic. In the Krajisnik case, Mr. Nielsen's testimony and report were referenced several times in the judgement, and we think it shows that that Trial Chamber found his evidence to be reliable and probative. So those are factors we think you can take into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As I understand Mr. Zecevic's objection, it rather goes to the fact that Mr. Nielsen is an analyst. He doesn't -- he doesn't purport to possess any expertise as such, and that for that reason we should not have him come as an expert but only as a normal viva voce witness, and would I like to hear you out on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have a definition of expert in our rules in this Tribunal. In my domestic jurisdiction, an expert is someone whom by virtue of education, training, experience, has some sort of specialised knowledge that can be useful in helping the jury or the Judges, the trier of fact, in resolving a pertinent issue in the case. In my jurisdiction as well, we have another category of a witness, somewhere between the percipient fact witness, the eyewitness to the bank robbery and an expert witness at the top, we have another category of witness that sometimes referred to as a summary witness which oftentimes may be someone like an analyst who reviews large collections of documents and then is able to provide some kind of summary and report about those large collections of documents. And they're treated somewhat in between how an expert is treated and a fact witness. In many ways some of the experts witnesses that we've had in the Tribunal here who worked in LRT, the Leadership Research Team, MAT, the Military Analysis Team, are what I was familiar with in my jurisdictions as summary witnesses, but would I argue that they do have some expertise because of the amount of time they've spent going over thousands of documents, and they just don't read the documents. Oftentimes they're familiar with the events from having read newspaper accounts, sometimes from their own personal experiences during the times of the conflict, from reviewing witness statements in some cases, and they do have information that's helpful to you. I think the objection raised by the Defence really is a matter that can be dealt with by you all at the end of the case when you've heard all the evidence, deciding how much weight to give it, and it should not bar him being called as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I mean, for the Chamber the main issue is that if ultimately Mr. Nielsen ends up being called as an expert, there's a difference in the manner in which he can be examined both by you as the calling party and by the Defence. We have raised a couple of times here that one of those differences exactly is the ability of the expert to provide opinions, which an ordinary fact witness would not be allowed to. So -- so this is why I'm fishing a bit to hear your arguments why we should allow Nielsen to come as an expert with, among other things, the possibility of providing an opinion about the matters that are put to him and of the Trial Chamber's reliance upon his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I understand your point, Your Honour. I think I've heard it expressed by at least one Judge in talking about some of these experts, that's like, well, what makes him an expert other than the fact that he sat there and read 10.000 documents over the past two years. I could do the same. And I say, yes, that's right, Judge, you could, and in my view, then you would be an expert. If I wanted some information about that issue and you had read 10.000 documents for two years, I would give your opinion more weight than I would somebody who hasn't seen it. In my domestic jurisdiction as well, we have certain kinds of issues that lay opinion is permissible on, things that fall within the common everyday experience of the average citizen. So in a drunk driving case in America, a witness can come in and even though he's not an expert like the police officer who may have -- the highway patrolman who has training in gauging drunk driving by giving people field sobriety tests and other things that the average person doesn't, but an average person has enough experience from everyday life to express an opinion about whether or not a person appeared to be under the influence of alcohol on that occasion. So I think again it's a matter that should to the weight you give his opinion, but I think he can be an expert. I guess it depends partly on how you define the area of expertise. And his area of expertise is about the MUP because he's examined these thousands of documents about the MUP and has read evidence of statements by people from the MUP and evidence about how the MUP worked during the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly the kind of information I was expecting from you. You had another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, concerning the timing of calling Dr. Nielsen. I fully understand the point raised by Mr. Zecevic, and as the lawyer who is scheduled to lead Dr. Nielsen's direct exam, I would prefer, personally, to have his testimony all in one block. I know in my last trial I had the experience sometimes where we had witnesses testify, called by the Defence, and I had to cross-examine where we didn't have English translations of some of the documents that were used with the witness. And it's a very difficult, almost impossible job to do and feel like I'm doing my job professionally because the witness may read out the paragraph 5 in the document, and the Defence says, "So that's the part -- that's the part we want." Well, I can't read the rest of the document. I can't put paragraph 5 in context, and it's not very satisfying to say well, when you get the English translation if you find something you would have wanted, well, maybe we'll call them back later. That's not very efficient or effective, and I don't think you want to work that way. But I'm on the horns of a dilemma and the Prosecution is on the horns of a dilemma here because in this case where we're prosecuting the minister of the interior and a chief of one of the regional security centres, high-ranking police individuals, we thought it important in our case to try to get you Judges as much information as possible early on in the case about what the MUP was and how it works. And so I'm torn between those two things: One, our desire to get you expert evidence and as much evidence as possible about the MUP early in the case, and that ability to be able to have his examination go straight through and be able to do my redirect examination with English translations of the documents that are used by the Defence. What I'd like to do is consult with the rest of my team and take to heart your suggestions about calling him later rather than earlier, but it may cause us problems with scheduling because we've tentatively planned him to be the first witness on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before you consult with Mrs. Korner, I would like to add that it might actually be beneficial to the Chamber to hear him later on, because through the next witnesses whom you will then call, we might, you know, pick up some more information about the MUP. At this early stage of the trial, we are very open to the scenery and to the scope of the indictment, and as we go along with the witnesses, you know, we learn more about the case, and so postponing Nielsen might not actually be such a bad idea, because that will make us better prepared to understand fully and appreciate his testimony when we get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take that point, Your Honour. I think that was something that came up in our internal discussions, too, and I think that's a valid point. We will consult and we will let you know as soon as possible what we propose to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The other difficulty has to do with his personal schedule and his teaching schedule, but I will have to speak to him about that. That's another factor for us. It's difficult to find a time when he's available, but we'll take that all into account and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Anyone from the Defence teams wishes to raise any point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm so sorry. Mr. Hannis was going to deal with that but there are perhaps a couple of small points that perhaps I ought to deal with now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise, Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We'll finish with you first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First is this: I omitted to ask for Dr. Donia's reports to become exhibits at the end of my examination-in-chief. So can I formally ask that that be made, the three reports, and that part of the Sarajevo report that you've allowed in. The second matter was this: And that was the question of the -- the motion that we filed asking for the admission of further documents on to the 65 ter list, and we then had a hearing in which we dealt with the Sarajevo report, and Your Honour then ruled that -- from the transcript, and I've forgotten what the date -- yes, 15th of September, Tuesday, the 15th of September, golly, only two days ago, that the certain parts of the report would be out, and in relation to the documents, the 29 documents included in your motion, it follows from the first of those 29 those will go. Now, we read that as meaning that the other documents were in, the ones that you've marked for identification which were part of our application to add these documents to the 65 ter list, and this is where I think the confusion arose. It's right to say that I didn't stand up and Your Honour didn't specifically either say in terms, "And those are the only ones we're excluding," but that's where the confusion arose. Obviously my application is that those documents which came from his earlier report footnotes should be admitted as exhibits. Now, can I say I'm not asking Your Honour to give a ruling about that straightaway but just to make the position clear, and I think that's where the confusion arose. Which leads me on to really a general point, if I may, Judge -- Your Honours. Unfortunately, particularly in the last week or so, there's been a lot of confusion because there's been a huge number of motions coming in, particularly from the Defence, and as Your Honours know and I needn't remind you, there are still a large number of outstanding matters to be ruled upon, but we -- at the moment we've been getting sort of rulings via e-mail as opposed to an order or a ruling, and it's not always easy to work out from that what it is that's being ruled upon or what we're being told to do. And one of the examples was we applied for the motion for -- we applied for Your Honours to reconsider your decision that we should reduce the witness list. We simply got an e-mail from the legal officer saying all deadlines stood without saying the motion for reconsideration therefore was not being granted. The Defence then say, because when we filed our reduced witness list, and we made it clear that we were doing so effectively, I must say, under protest but we were doing it because that was the order, and with the caveats that if we couldn't reach agreement, for example, on exhumations, that we would be reapplying to put these witnesses back in. The Defence then filed a motion saying it's moot, but they object to it anyhow, and we haven't actually had, as it were, a ruling. And Your Honours, I appreciate it's all because it's been rather chaotic over the last few weeks, but could we make a plea that we get proper orders, however short, but proper orders and proper filed decisions from Your Honours rather than decisions through e-mail from the legal officers obviously forwarding on Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Certainly. It goes without saying. May I just add that for the mail that you received from the legal officer, I don't think that was an order in any way. It was an indication of what is obvious, namely, that the time-limits stand as they were ordered. Your motion for reconsideration is still on the table and we'll get to it. Now, as of today we have ten days of a break, and we will use, certainly, that time to clear up as many of the outstanding motions as we possibly can, and the Defence will use the time to prepare for its further re-examination of your witnesses. We expect to hear from you very soon whether you will accommodate our suggestion to postpone Nielsen, and if you do so, then who will then be your next witness, and the Defence will need to start preparing for that and so will we. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which leads actually on to the next issue and that's the question of timing. Your Honour said in the Pre-Trial Conference -- I had that up some -- yes. The Prosecution would have 212 hours. The Defence will altogether be given the same amount of time, 212 hours. So we're taking it that's the same. And I'm taking it that, therefore, they get the equal amount of time to cross-examine as we get to call in chief. It wasn't perhaps altogether clear. But we do need to know how long each -- the Defence are going to get to cross-examine the witnesses before they come, because we get -- we get a lot of problems with VWS about trying to organise the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As soon as we have had a look according to your motion for reconsideration -- had a second look at the order to reduce the number of witnesses to 131, then we will also set time for the Defence. We would like to have indications from the Defence teams as to how long they wish to have in relation to the 131 witnesses that have now been tabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if I -- if I may be briefly heard on the subject. Now, the situation with the 92 ter witnesses is such that it -- that it's going to be and it is in practice on a case-to-case basis. What I mean to say is the following: The Prosecution, the amount of time that the Prosecution uses in court actually to introduce the witness might be -- might be very short, because the Prosecutor used enormous amount of time talking to the witness, preparing his statement. Now if -- so the correlation between the time that the Prosecution uses in court actually to bring the witness and to offer his 92 ter statement cannot be compared to the need of the -- of the Defence to cross-examine the witness, because in fact they have been able to talk to the witness for many days and prepare the statement, and there are some -- there might be some really important, relevant issues in his statement that we need to address. Plus the proofing notes, which usually are coming, plus, of course, some other issues. So I don't think that we will be able to give you a general number or any estimation on any of the witnesses or generally for all witnesses, because it is, as I say, on a case-to-case basis, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The whole idea behind allowing witnesses to come under 92 ter is to save time by not having to go through the examination-in-chief in which or during which the witness would say everything that is already included in his statement. So as to avoid repetition of that kind. The statements have been provided, submitted to the Defence teams. So they, each of the two Defence teams, are fully aware of what this witness will say. It's possible that proofing notes may come in at a very late stage, but the Prosecution is under an obligation to provide those as soon as possible, and in any case I wouldn't expect proofing notes to depart radically from what is already included in the statements. So my point is this: The Defence teams know -- the Defence teams know that -- what's coming up from -- from each witness. We have also told in the procedural guidelines that we will not, in general, allow the Prosecution to spend very much time in introducing the 92 ter witnesses, somewhere between - I can't remember - 15 or 30 minutes is what the Prosecution will have, unless there are particular other grounds for deviating from that, but very short time to introduce the witness and then the witness is transferred to you. I don't see why you cannot, by going through the statements, make an estimation of how much time you wish to have to cross-examine this witness on the basis of what is in his testimony. And it is on a case-by-case basis. Sometimes you may wish to have only 30 minutes. Sometimes you may wish to have five hours. That's fine, but please indicate to us so that we have something from you when we determine how much time ultimately will be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I understood -- I understood -- I'm sorry. I understood, Your Honours, that you wish us to indicate now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm inviting you to, as soon as you can, within hopefully the end of this week, if possible, or maybe early next week, but as soon as you can, to give us an indication of how much time you would wish to have with each of the 131 witnesses that are on the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. All we're asking for at this stage is for the witness we have to notify two weeks in advance to VWS, so we would like an order, please, actually, by Friday or Monday at the latest, depending on whether we have to reschedule because of your indication about Dr. Nielsen, how much time the Defence require for each of the scheduled witnesses who are due to come. And we'd like that -- we're not asking for the whole lot at the moment, just the next batch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well -- thank you very much, Mrs. Korner. That makes it actually easier. So if you can have the -- if you can give us the indication of the time you and Mr. Zupljanin wishes to have for the witnesses that will be scheduled to come in the near future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as soon as we receive the schedule of witnesses, we might be able to provide, but, Your Honours, again I -- this is going to be in a very general terms. We don't want to be bound by -- by our promise, because with can happen is that one of the witnesses who comes first raises an issue which we have to explore with the second and the third witness because they might be coming from the very same municipality. So it is -- the case is one living thing. I mean, it is developing during the case, so the testimony's in the other court -- I know you know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to give my argument some sense. I'm sorry if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. I'm -- we are fully aware of the practical problems, but by the end of the day a decision has to be made, because there is a planning issue that needs to be -- to be issued. VWS needs to know how many days or -- the witness is going to be here. So I know it's difficult, but sooner or later a decision will have to be made. What we will do is that we will assess the witnesses as well, and we will have our own opinion as to how much time we think the Defence might need. In addition to that, we invite the Defence teams to also come forward with their indication. And when we have that, we'll make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Once the decision is made, then the VWS can start planning for the travels of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will endeavour in providing the -- and accommodating the Trial Chamber and everybody else in that. I just want to say this for the record: I don't think that -- that there is -- there is a correlation between the fairness of the trial and any kind of timing needs of VWS or whoever in -- in that respect. One other matter, Your Honour. We wanted to be heard on -- on what -- if we may reply to what Mr. Hannis just raised about Mr. Nielsen, Nielsen's testimony. Briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If you have some important things to add, then we would invite you to come forward with them right away, but please be short because we're running out of time. As you can see we have six minutes left --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- and we still have one decision to render.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan will do the submission, very shortly, briefly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before you take the floor, Mr. O'Sullivan, can I raise another issue which the Chamber discussed previously, namely, about the standing of counsels before the Chamber. I think that the ordinary rule is -- or the ordinary practice, at least, is that it is only counsel and co-counsel that can address the Court, and that the reason for this is really that we have the power of attorney from the defendants to those counsels. Now, if the counsels wish to have other members of their team appear before the Court that's perfectly fine with us, but as a matter of order, I would suggest that whenever you wish Mr. O'Sullivan or anyone else from your team to address the Court that you ask for permission to do so. I am also aware of the fact that Mr. O'Sullivan's position is special because he's really a reserve counsel, so we will address that, but -- but as a general rule, I think it is appropriate to just clear it up with the Chamber before anyone else but yourself and your co-counsel takes the floor and addresses the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, due to the specific situation, which you are aware of and I would not like to come into, I specifically asked OLAD on the appointment of Mr. O'Sullivan that he be appointed as a co-counsel. There is no limit how many counsels can one of the defendants have in the rules, I think, because the Prosecution is represented by five or six counsels, so, so can -- so can the Defence as well, I believe. And I requested that specifically due to the specificum of the situation, as you're aware, and that is why I didn't thought that it -- it needed an additional request -- needed an additional permission from the Trial Chamber to -- but we will act accordingly, yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Rest assured that we will always be interested in hearing what Mr. O'Sullivan has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And we give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's late in the day and I'll be very brief. I just wanted to respond to a couple of your questions that you put to Mr. Hannis regarding the expert. We share his definition of what an expert is; it's someone who by virtue of his or her knowledge, skill or background can assist you in deciding issues, live issues, between the parties. But this implies someone who does have this objective or scientific background which Mr. Nielsen does not have. That's the first point. Second point is in relation to his former employment by the Office of the Prosecutor. There is precedent that says that if current or former employee of the Office of the Prosecutor can testify. I wish, however, to point out that there is precedent going the other way, in particular in the Milutinovic case, in the case of Mr. Coo. And the third and final point I wish to make is that I must take issue with what Mr. Hannis says, that because someone has read 10.000 pages or documents that makes them an expert. Your Honour, I'm not a civil engineer and I could read 10.000 documents on bridge construction, but I don't think you'd want to drive across the bridge that I told you was safe. So it's more than just the fact that someone is intelligent and that they can read. It's by virtue of special knowledge, training, or experience that they can be -- they can be an expert and they should be objective and detached from one of the parties and certainly not an employee who is active in the conduct and prosecution of a case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. We'll take note of your input to this question. I have one last ruling to make, and that is the ruling to admit the three -- or the two and a half expert reports by Dr. Donia. We hereby agree that they should be admitted, and we ask the Registrar to provide an exhibit number to them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those will be Exhibits P30, P31, and P32, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and unless any of the parties have any other issues to raise -- hold on a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Our legal officer reminds us that -- and you may sit. I know of your conditions with your foot, Madam Korner. You had asked for clarification of the oral ruling that was made the other day regarding what is admitted and what is not admitted from the Sarajevo report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, from -- from the marked for identification -- from the exhibits which came from the footnotes of the others reports. That's what I'm trying to get sorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The admission of those three documents was -- was MFI'd because there was uncertainty about whether or not they were included in the ruling. The ruling was that the documents that were mentioned in the footnotes of the three chapters of the Sarajevo report which we did admit were also admissible, whereas documents in other parts of the Sarajevo report were not admissible, and so we MFI'd the three pieces because we weren't sure of whether or not they were inside or outside the three chapters, and when we find out whether they were or not, the MFI status will be settled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It -- and that's -- that's one of the difficulties I've been referring to about not having written [indiscernible]. We put in a motion asking for a lot of the documents that -- in fact, that all the documents that Dr. Donia specifically covered should be admitted. You then gave a ruling excluding from that long list any documents that came within the chapters of the report that you weren't allowing in. We therefore assumed that that was a ruling on the whole motion and therefore you were allowing us to add the other documents, nothing to do with the Sarajevo report, but to do with the earlier two reports which were footnoted but hadn't been added to the 65 ter list before, and that's what I -- and, as I say, we're quite happy for you to consider it because I see the time, but that's what I'm trying to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I suggest we rule on it in writing. It's already over the time, and I suggest we adjourn now, and we will reconvene here on Tuesday, the 29th of September, and that is in the afternoon. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of September, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 25
